democracy and political accountability in candidate countries. In other words,
the conditionality process weakened democratic deliberation but strengthened
democratic institutional designs in those countries. The harmonization of EU and
national legal systems happened as a rapid fast-tracked process of importation
of laws but it also permanently affected legal and political institutions. It thus
contributed to the much slower and ongoing process of transformating the legal
and political cultures of candidate states, involving changes in the argumentative
styles of the judiciary, administrative governance and so on.
During the 1990s, post-communist countries reinvented their national
sovereignty, drafted new constitutional documents, and subsequently used their
newly built constitutional sovereignty in EU membership negotiations. With
the exception of Hungary and Poland, post-communist states joining the EU in
2004 had all been ‘new states’ — Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania reconstituted their
statehood against the background of the collapsing Soviet Union, Slovenia left
behind former republics of Yugoslavia in violent turmoil, and the Czech Republic
and Slovakia peacefully abandoned common Czechoslovak federal statehood. For
these states, EU membership was yet another form of their new existence and a
proof of their identity in the world of international politics and law.
In contrast to the post-1989 process of rebuilding the constitutional sovereignty
and national independence of post-communist countries, the EU requires its
member states to delegate substantial sovereign powers to its institutions, including
monetary policy, foreign affairs, border controls, judicial power, policing and so
on. In all post-communist countries, these sovereign powers have been in the
process of being reconstituted since 1989, yet they were coevally limited during
the accession process.
This process of self-limitation of constitutional sovereignty was intended to
cement rather than weaken the liberal democratic rule of law at post-communist
nation-state level. Nevertheless, it also revealed structural shortcomings of the EU
as a supranational organization reaching far beyond a common international law
framework, yet falling short of any form of federal or confederative democratically
legitimate statehood. It is not surprising, therefore, that the issue of constitutional
sovereignty and its limits has returned as the most prominent constitutional problem
in the wake of the EU accession of former post-communist states. The public, its
political representatives and various constitutional bodies have gradually begun to
emphasize the need to protect national statehood, associating it closely with the
protection of constitutional democracy and human rights.”
Reflecting on the prominent position of constitutional courts during post-
communist transformations and the legalist character of EU integration, it is
clear how these judicial bodies became a centre for constitutional debates.
Constitutional ambivalence about the accession process was addressed differently
by different constitutional courts in different post-communist countries. As

early as 1998, the Hungarian Constitutional Court raised the question of the
legitimacy of the harmonization process in its ‘Europe Agreement Case’, in which
it reasserted constitutional sovereignty of the Republic of Hungary against the
direct applicability of EU law and stated that a transfer of sovereignty to a foreign
legal system needed to be explicitly authorized under the Hungarian constitutional
rule.*? In the judgment, it also emphasized that the constitutional amendment must
follow the prescribed constitutional procedure rather than be stealthily enforced
by means of parliamentary ratification of an international treaty.
Similarly, the Slovenian Constitutional Court argued that ‘the Constitution
places the public interest, for the State not to commit itself under international
law to fulfil obligations which are not in conformity with its Constitution, at the
level of a constitutional value’.** Should the court find some provisions of an
international treaty unconstitutional, the ratification would be subject to the state’s
reservations being added to the treaty, its renegotiation or to a prior constitutional
amendment.
It is interesting to see how constitutional courts’ commitment to the rule of law
and constitutional sovereignty during the accession process opened up a debate
which logically followed the 1993 German Constitutional Court’s ‘Maastricht
Case’ decision, addressing the same problems from the perspective of a court of
a member state.* In this landmark decision, German judges discussed the wide
technical implications of the political fact that there is no European demos and that
the EU, therefore, falls short of the substantive democratic legitimation necessary
for any project of supranational statehood based on the supremacy of its legal
system.** In what has become known as the Kompetenz der Kompetenz dilemma,
the court reiterated its ultimate power to review and protect constitutional rights of
German citizens, even against the EU.
Constitutional courts of Central and Eastern European candidate states
originally interpreted the relationship between EU and national legal systems
as a matter of intergovernmental negotiations drawing on national mechanisms
of democratic legitimization. However, since the accession of post-communist
countries to the EU in 2004, jurisprudence and theory of EU law in those countries
has been witnessing much more diverse doctrinal responses to the process of EU

the constitutions, created for setting in motion a mostly goal-oriented period
of transition, are destined to adjust, in a second phase, their instrumental parts,
characterized by a more mature treatment of the necessary tools. It is thus
not surprising that the second phase of transition becomes more ambiguous
in relation to the selection of tools, and hence more open to various concrete
outcomes. For a socio-legal scholar, this period of transition can be imagined
as a journey towards high mountains. First seen on the horizon they will orient
the traveller like a polar star, but from a shorter distance, they will reveal an
increasing number of alternatives and probably, after a lapse of time, other
mountains will be discovered beyond.
The revision and adaptation to social reality of the norms adopted by CEE
countries are worked out principally by different internal legal cultures. As in a
trial and error process, jurists, judges and legal scholars attempt, where necessary,
to correct legal norms, even constitutional norms, taking into consideration their
possible negative effects. This is true not only in common law countries, but also
in continental Europe, where the great importance of producing adjustments in
the legal order, through the so called Juristenrecht, is increasingly recognized.
Like a beach constantly submerged and levelled by the sea, legal orders, including
constitutions, are continuously corrected and rendered homogeneous with the
newly emerging interests, by recurrent waves of legal decisions.
This phase of transition in CEE countries must, in a pragmatic process, tackle
the new external and internal requirements of the ‘post-communist’ era. But what
does it really mean to be in a post-communist era? It was observed that, whereas
in a first phase the expression semantically accentuates the suffix communist,
suggesting that ‘the communist past, or its legacies, retain[s] present effects’, ina
second phase the emphasis seems to be on the prefix post, suggesting that ‘we can
regard the communist past as some sort of dream or nightmare, which dissipates
on waking’. This means that the search for constitutional stabilization, under
the pressures of an increasing process of differentiation among social systems
formerly integrated by a totalitarian regime, must be supported by corresponding
legal cultures. In this phase for CEE countries, the main sources of variety are
the vague definition of ‘programmes and projects’ concerning the EU as a whole
and the differentiated local effects of the first wave of regulations following the
indications of the EU. This is a process destined to continue, within an interstatal
framework, at the level of law operators. In this context, differentiation and
integration could both be reinforced.

From the point of view of social systems theory, the development of a higher
level of self-reflection is closely connected with the mechanism of autopoiesis, which
emerged in advanced legal orders as an instrument for triggering legal evolution.
The active presence of a second level of observation, which this approach implies,
allows a normative order to assume a cognitive orientation in order to correct its
inefficient norms. All this presupposes that legal systems explicitly produce a certain
amount of ‘redundancies’,“ from among which legal professionals could select,
introducing, when necessary, further adjustments. This does not necessarily imply
a loss of importance of the normative characteristics of the legal system; simply a
mutual acknowledgment of legal and non-legal systems. Only if economic logic is
recognized by legal logic, and vice versa, will a channel of selective communication
among these social systems become more than a pure utopia or a sort of normative
invasion. In particular, the legal system seems capable of producing an increasing
economization of itself, through the ability of legal decision-makers to translate into
their own code the criteria of rationality adopted by economic actors.
In order to ensure an adequate basis for describing intersystemic communication,
a new legal semantics must take into consideration the typical media and cultural
points of reference of the socially mostrelevant sectors (politics, economy, religion).
They could selectively ‘irritate’, through the mediation of their operators, legal
professionals, who could then react, relying ‘on their own network of operations’.
In other words, the ‘operative closure’ of every system does not mean isolation,
but a self-referential way of defining ‘what belongs to the system and what belongs
to the environment’. Obviously, this refers to the influence of social systems on
the legal system, and vice versa. The media connected to law, politics, economy
and religion (legality, power, utility and faith) could thus respectively underline
their cultural orientations (justice, consensus, profit, conscience) and contribute in
this way to a gradual co-evolution of the different parts of the whole social system.
Table 2.7 provides an illustration of this.
From this perspective, the cognitive and innovative potential of the legal system,
based not so much on a hierarchical relation to society but on a more flexible and
interactive concept of law, is particularly visible when more attention is given to the
functioning of the other social systems. Starting from the presupposition that even
the most distant sectors of society could converge, especially when the normative
points of reference are so abstract, as in the case of constitution,“ the legal system
could play explicitly the role of the final factor of coordination for the different
social systems, of a sort of ‘meta-communicator’ able to understand the different
languages and typical codes of communication of the other social systems.

example, the Czech Republic and Russia); and a shared system of appointment,
with different bodies (for example, the president, the parliament and a judicial
representative body) having its own ‘share’ of judges (one-third) to appoint (for
example, Romania and Bulgaria). Second, the list of authorized initiators is
quite diverse, varying from country to country, but typically including a group
(defined by a number or percentage) of members of parliament, the president,
the government, the ombudsman and so on. Third, the dominant type of review
is abstract and ex post, though most of the CEE states also have a ‘concrete’ path
of review (initiated by an ‘ordinary’ court encountering a constitutionally dubious
legal rule in the process of hearing the case) and occasionally an ex ante review
(for example, in Poland, initiated by the President, and also in Romania). Fourth,
all the CEE states’ decisions of constitutional review are now final, in the sense
that there is no possibility of an appeal or override, though until recently there
were the possibilities of parliamentary override in Poland and Romania.’
This chapter will reflect upon the impact of those constitutional courts upon
constitutional culture in CEE, viewed from the perspective of their relationship
with the other branches of government, in particular, the legislatures. It will adopt
a simple, commonsensical understanding of constitutional culture as the degree
to which a constitution matters in a given polity: the degree to which important
collective decisions are in fact informed by constitutional constraints; and the
degree to which the society as a whole considers constitutional strictures as
significant and worth considering when evaluating proposed or actual collective
decisions. This is, of course, a very simplified, perhaps simplistic understanding
of ‘constitutional culture’ but, for the purposes of this chapter, it is as good a point
of departure as any.
The initial hypothesis is that the ‘activism’ of constitutional courts (a term
which will be clarified below) can have both adverse and positive impacts upon
constitutional culture, understood in a way just articulated. On the one hand,
strong constitutional courts may encourage and consolidate the feeling (erroneous,
in my view), both among political actors and in a community at large, that all
other branches of government are free to disregard constitutional strictures and
should take into account only policy considerations because, if they contravene
the constitutional norms, a strong constitutional court will intervene and correct
the decision in a constitutional way. This is the adverse impact of the existence
and activities of robust constitutional courts on constitutional culture. On the other
hand, strong constitutional courts act as a powerful incentive for the executive and
legislative branch to factor constitutional values into their decisions (because the
prospect of a judicial override is politically costly), and also as an actual guarantee
that an unconstitutional decision sooner or later (usually ‘sooner’, in a system of

matter, common sense probably dictates that the significance of overturning a law
on abortion, capital punishment or lustration is higher than that of overturning a
law striking down a particular procedure for obtaining professional recognition as
a practising lawyer. In terms of the nature of the reasoning — the second criterion
— the above emphasis, ‘within the set of argumentative resources available to it’, is
deliberate. It is safe to assume that any court usually has some leeway of choice of
an argumentative method which may support different conclusions. This is most
evident when a court engages in a proportionality analysis — one of the favourite
methods of constitutional courts, especially when the admissibility of legislative
restrictions of constitutional rights is scrutinized. Proportionality analysis — and
its twin tool, the balancing of constitutional values ~ is a method which ultimately
may support either of two contrasting results in any given case, depending on the
comparative weight assigned by a judge to competing constitutional values. As
these weights are not — and cannot be — strictly prescribed by the constitutional
text, the judges, within the set of argumentative resources available to them, may
end up either upholding or striking down a challenged law. The tendency to do
the latter rather than the former is an easy, commonsensical symptom of judicial
activism.
Factors Affecting the ‘Strength’ of Judicial Review
To ascertain the relationship between the legislature and the constitutional
court, it is possible to talk about the ‘strength’ of judicial review. This refers to
the quantitative and qualitative dimensions of confrontations between the court
and the law-makers, reflected in the number of successful referrals to the court
(particularly by the parliamentary minority) and also in the relative importance of
the laws invalidated for unconstitutionality. This is just another way of discussing
‘judicial activism’. The strength has a quantitative dimension — a dimension of
scope that refers to the range of issues within which the court’s preferences collide
with those of the parliament — and a qualitative dimension, that is, the salience of
the issues that produce disagreement between the two institutions. There are many
factors determining both the range and the significance of the clash between court
and parliament; obviously, the institutional rules of access to the constitutional
court and the range of actors entitled to initiate the review are among the more
important ones.
The starting point of the analysis has to be the nature of the constitutional
courts themselves. Irrespectively of whether one describes the constitutional courts
as judicial bodies of a special type, or quasi-legislative institutions, the political
dimension of the courts’ activity is obvious. Firstly, there is an unavoidable
connection with the political sphere, since the constitutional courts are often
being asked to decide on matters that have great impact on the politics of the day.
Secondly, and more controversially, the fact that politicians, either exclusively
Constitutional Courts and Constitutional Culture 103
or predominantly, as is the case in the ‘divided’ or shared systems of judicial
appointments,’ elect judges might cast doubts on the political neutrality of the
latter. Jt might also be used as a convenient argument against an unfavourable
ruling by politicians who have lost their courtroom battles. In other words, there is
an inevitable conundrum inscribed in the very concept and design of constitutional
review. Consequently, the constitutional courts in the CEE region have had to face
various challenges resulting form their dual, legal-political nature while carving
out for themselves a place on the political scene. These processes have taken
different forms in individual countries. They have been influenced by several
factors, some of which could be described as country-specific, others as universal
to the CEE region.
First, the very design of a constitutional court has a great impact upon the
relationship between the court and other branches of the government. For instance,
in Romania the availability of the ex ante control of the laws resulted in a specific
perception of the role of the Constitutional Court by politicians. Parliamentary
groups of senators or deputies most often initiated preventive control. Proposals
for legislative acts were brought before the Court not so much in order to control
their constitutionality as to secure the interests of political parties. In effect, as a
Romanian constitutional expert opined, the Court was cast in the role of arbiter of
political disputes of the day and exposed to political pressures.® Also, the fact that
the Court’s decisions until 2003 did not enjoy a final binding force and could be
overturned by a majority of two-thirds of both chambers of the Parliament created a
particular situation. The rulings of the Court were regarded as yet another, perhaps
more authoritative, opinion on the law debated by the Parliament, but not as ultimate
legal decisions about contested issues. Yet, despite these institutional factors, the
Romanian Constitutional Court managed to gain the respect and acceptance of its
political actors.’ The case of the Romanian Court will be discussed, in more detail,
in a later part of this chapter.

constitutional court. Almost all consolidated democracies of CEE have opted for a
parliamentary system with a relatively weak presidency. An exception is Poland,
with its semi-presidential system, where the presidential veto power has indeed at
times effectively released the Constitutional Tribunal from the need to consider
(and, putatively, invalidate) controversial laws. However, not all of the powers
of this relatively strong presidency are capable of weakening the legislature-
constitutional court clash; indeed, the presidential power to initiate an ex ante
review (incidentally, also present in Hungary) may exacerbate the disagreements,
because the burden of invalidation then falls on the Constitutional Tribunal rather
than on the President.
The other Central European consolidated democracies assign a weaker role to
the president within the parliamentary system than Poland. In some cases, even
though the president may be elected directly by citizens, implying a relatively
high degree of political legitimacy, for example in Slovenia, he nonetheless
does not possess any power of veto over legislation approved by parliament. In
neither Hungary nor Lithuania does the president enjoy such a power of veto
(even though Lithuania is often classified as an instance of semi-presidentialism,
owing to the fact that the president has reasonably strong powers in the field of
international relations, dissolution of assembly and legislative initiative). The
presidential powers of veto in Estonia, Romania (another state often classified
as semi-presidential) and Slovakia are more limited than in Poland, because in
these countries his suspensive veto can be overridden by a simple parliamentary
majority rather than by a qualified majority of three-fifths as is the case in Poland
(in Bulgaria and the Czech Republic an absolute majority is required); hence the
capacity of presidents to act as ‘veto points’ is more limited in these countries.
All of this illustrates that, with the exception of Poland and, to a lesser degree, the
Czech Republic and Bulgaria, the institution of president does not really constitute
a significant ‘veto point’ affecting the strength of judicial review.
Apart from the president, another ‘veto point’ may reside in an upper chamber
which may be effective in screening out the most problematic pieces of legislation,
thus reducing the potential for conflict between the constitutional court and the
parliament. In two of the Central European bi-cameral systems (Poland and the
Czech Republic) the powers of the upper chambers are more limited than those of
the lower chambers, as they possess only suspending vetoes vis-a-vis legislation
(although, unlike the Senates in France or Spain whose veto can be overridden by
simple majority of the lower chambers, the Senate’s veto in Poland and the Czech
Republic can be overridden only by an absolute majority thereof). In the third bi-
cameral Central European system, in Romania, both chambers possess the same
legislative powers. This, of course, renders the Senate much more significant and
effective as a ‘veto point’ than the Polish or Czech Senates, especially owing to
the fact that, in practice, the two chambers often compete with one another for
Constitutional Courts and Constitutional Culture 107
the final word on particular pieces of legislation.'° Nonetheless, even the merely
suspending veto of the Polish or Czech Senates may, at times, deflect the force of
the clash between the lower chamber and the Constitutional Court. An example is
provided by the Czech Republic, in which the Senate occasionally sides with the
Constitutional Court when the latter collides with the lower chamber. This may be
partly owing to the fact that Czech senators are less bound by strict party discipline
than the members of the lower chamber, and also because the relatively long term
of senators’ office (six years) brings their perspective closer to that of the judges
of the Constitutional Court. (In this respect the Czech Senate is different from the
Polish and Romanian Senates, where the term of office for senators is the same as
for members of the lower chamber, that is, four years.) There have therefore been
cases in which the Senate has formed an ‘alliance’ with the Constitutional Court
against the lower chamber.
As an example, consider the Czech law of 1998, which reduced the salaries
of public servants by annulling the traditional ‘salary supplement’ (the so-called
‘13th and 14th monthly pays’) for all public employees, as part of the government’s
austerity measures. The Constitutional Court protested against the inclusion
of judges’ salaries in these restrictions, on the basis of judicial independence,
and also on the basis of the special role played by judges in the protection of
democratic values and the rule of law.’ As a consequence, the Court rewrote the
law by exempting judges from the universal pay reduction. The Court’s decision
was, as could be expected, unpopular with the general public and with politicians,
including President Havel who went as far as to criticize the judgment publicly.
The following year, the Assembly of Deputies (the lower chamber) enacted the
austerity law, which basically replicated the previous year’s measures, including
the removal of pay supplements for judges. At this point, the Senate returned the
law to the Assembly specifically on the basis that the parliament should respect
the decision of the Constitutional Court. The Assembly chose, however, to ignore
both the position of the Senate and the earlier decision of the Court (which had
applied to an earlier, although relevantly similar, law) and enacted the 1999 law
in its original form. This new statute came again before the Constitutional Court
which, by this time, had changed its mind and found the law consistent with the
Constitution. In this case of a parliament-constitutional court clash, it was the
Court which eventually caved in, but not before discovering an ally in the upper
chamber of the parliament, and realizing that its objections had been endorsed by
the upper chamber and, presumably, considered seriously by the lower one.

less weight on the coherence and integrity of the law,’ and more weight on the
implications of judicial decisions in terms of political morality as it is broadly
understood. Several preliminary notes are in order.
First, in contrast to the Hungarian Constitutional Court, the BCC did not embark
on a massive effort of ‘harmonization’ of doctrines and theories of interpretation
with the leading European courts. On the contrary, much of the jurisprudence of
the Bulgarian judges remains context-dependent and even idiosyncratic. More
importantly, in terms of doctrine- and theory-creation the Bulgarian judges
remain decidedly minimalist and, in general, the court could be described as
‘self-restricting’.* Yet this does not mean that the court has not been involved in
important disputes. On the contrary, certain policy areas, such as the restitution
of properties nationalized under the communist regime, regulation of public
electronic media, judicial independence and self-government, and many others
have been heavily affected by the jurisprudence of the BCC. Indeed, it could be
argued that, especially during the 1990s, the court was in an active dialogue with
the Bulgarian government and legislature in terms of policy-making.
Also, the doctrinal minimalism of the court does not mean that it has been
completely atheoretical. As Cass Sunstein has argued, judges often involve mid-
level theorizing in their search for under-theorized agreements in the process of
conflict-resolution.’ These mid-level theories could hardly survive strict scrutiny
in terms of coherence with the principles and rules of modern constitutionalism.
But often they prove quite helpful, and very often they are the best that judges
could hope for in certain circumstances.
Secondly, according to Bulgarian legal doctrines, judges do not have discretion®
— they cannot resort in their judicial decision-making to anything but the law,
which is supposed to provide them with a single right answer in every dispute.
Of course, in informal conversations some constitutional judges are inclined to
speak frankly about the difficulties of interpretation, and the challenges of de
facto judicial discretion. These judges are a minority on the Constitutional Court,
however, and the dominant views are militantly doctrinaire in this regard.

From the point of view of constitutional theory, one of the main questions which
minimalism raises is whether it is capable of encouraging a culture of respect for the
Constitution and general foundational norms of the Bulgarian community. Some
scholars have argued that respect for constitutional norms in Bulgaria is generally
very low. For example, in their thoughtful paper ‘Invisible contexts, invisible
barriers: The limits of the normative explanation of constitutional change’,”
Ralitsa Peeva and Ivan Krastev set out to cast doubt on the very possibility of a
general normative theory of constitutionalism in Bulgaria. Their main argument
was that the elaboration of such a general theory would require a ‘common
context of different constitutional choices’. Such a common context, they argued,
does not exist, which places a decisive limit on ‘normative constitutionalism’
and disables it as an analytical and explanatory tool. If one is to understand the
processes of constitution-making, as well as the workings of constitutionalism,
detailed contextual and historical analysis of the strategic choices of different
actors should be carried out. In this analysis even minute contextual factors could
have enormous explanatory power and would (sometimes) override the abstract,
principled explanations of ‘normative constitutionalism’.
Peeva and Krastev supported their major claim by embarking on an analysis of
five specific choices of Bulgarian constitutionalism: the timing of the constituent
assembly; the inclusion in the constitution of a ban on ethnic parties; the inclusion
of a vice-presidential institution; the number of MPs; and the age, citizenship and
residency conditions for presidential candidates. In all of these choices, the authors
argued, the constitution-drafters were not led by general normative principles of
constitutionalism, but by strategic considerations in the process of competing and
bargaining with their political opponents. All of these choices were the result of
deals, compromises and sometimes the consideration of seemingly irrelevant facts
(such as the seating capacity of the plenary hall of the building of the National
Assembly). Therefore, the authors claimed, general normative theory cannot
account for or explain these specific choices, a fact which illustrates its intrinsic
limitations.

Settling Accounts with the Past 157
with past human rights violations under the principle of the law-governed state
imposes legal definitions and reasoning on real-life situations, and subordinates
social and political actions to legal procedures. Thus, it fulfils the promise of
legality, so important at the beginning of a historical change. Moreover, it testifies
to the sincerity of the high moral standards with which CEE societies started their
transformation: living within the truth, and recognizing and compensating human
rights violations.
However, settling accounts with the past also concurrently introduces a serious
challenge to the principle of the law-governed state. First and foremost, not all
cases of human rights violation were punishable under the old law. Obviously,
collaborating with the former regime — internationally recognized as legal — or
with its secret police was not punishable at all. Therefore governments that
undertook the task of seriously dealing with the past found themselves forced
to reach beyond a literal understanding of the law-governed state principle.
They needed to bring in some ingenious methods for defining crimes and their
punishment in a process known as decommunization and/or lustration, that is, of
cleansing the public sector of high-ranking officials of the previous regime and
people tainted by collaboration with its policing organs. These methods came to be
known as transitory justice (Teitel, 2000). However, because of the often complex
and unclear nature of the cases, as well as of the evidence itself, when free access
to files is limited such methods easily turn into weapons in political struggles:
they are used to compromise political opponents. Furthermore, in the case of
the nationalization of property, that is, violation of property rights, restitution of
property necessitates economic sacrifice on the part of society and its government,
which have to compensate the losses, reprivatize public property, and find legal
solutions to often unsolvable problems.
In consequence, the very principle of the law-governed state is used and
misused by proponents and opponents of the reckoning with the past and opening
of files, because of its entirely contrasting interpretation: either as justification for
not dealing with it, or for dealing with it in a quite limited way; or as justification
for its thorough investigation and punishment of perpetrators and instigators
(Baranska, 2007: 112).
All these dilemmas overlap with those already characterized: the lack ofa clear
rupture in the process of regime transformation and the predominant lawyers’ (that
is, positivistic concept of legality) characterization of the legal culture and legal
education of Central and Eastern Europe.
As an outcome, dealing with past human rights violations contributes to the
ambiguities of transformation. First and foremost, it presents an unavoidable
challenge to post-communist constitutionalism: either it culminates in the
questioning of the law-governed state principle, at least in its most obvious, direct
meaning, or it leads to the reproduction of constitutional fiction and hypocrisy.
The remainder of this paper will briefly outline the most typical approaches
to the difficult task of past reckoning in Central and Eastern Europe, and the
arguments that justify each of them.
158 Central and Eastern Europe After Transition
Knowledge as Power: The Paradoxes of Democracy and Model Approaches
Itisno wonder that legacies of state crimes evoke burning questions for governments
and societies. These questions are still important in the countries in which the
transformation started. Dealing with the past and settling accounts with it means
deciding how new officials will treat the guilt of their predecessors. Evaluation
of a system leads to the evaluation of its functionaries and their collaborators.
Sometimes this ends in ‘naming’ and ‘shaming’, that is, in the stigmatization of
perpetrators, instigators and collaborators; sometimes it ends in the ‘cleansing’
of structures of government, the ‘ousting’ of compromised officials. If dealing
with the past is oriented towards prosecution and punishment — in all forms of
stigmatization, lustration and decommunization — one could cali such an approach
to the past ‘perpetrator-oriented’ (Skapska, 2003: 199-218)
Dealing with the past could also lead to compensating and honouring its
victims above all, and then to rectifying the wrongs committed by the former
regime as far as is possible. The right to truth could be particularly instrumental
as a basis for a ‘victim-oriented’ approach to the past. This could lead not only
to the ‘cleansing’ of social institutions, but also to the honouring of the victims’
dignity. The participation of victims in the procedures of truth-revealing and their
compensation for physical and psychological injuries, as well as the restitution of
property rights, restores their trust in law and justice and in the new government.
Thus, it has a great legitimizing potential, which is so crucial for new democracies.
It is further instrumental for victims to be involved in the process of post-communist,
democratic reconstruction. Hearing victims, making their experience a matter of
legal debate and, whenever such debates are made public, making their experience
a matter of public concern is of great potential in overcoming their isolation and
exclusion, and helping them out of the silence that surrounded them before, at least
in the public sphere. Moreover, it helps to overcome the deficits of the narrow law-
governed state principle interpretation by including human rights protection in it.’
Dealing with the past could also build a foundation for the reconstruction of social
bonds on the basis of reconciliation, and for the ‘healing’ of social wounds after
the truth about the past is made public.*
6 The perpetrator-oriented approach seems to be the most compatible with the
conventional understanding of the law-governed state principle. It also reflects some
cultural features of those societies in which it was initially conceptualized and introduced
into legal systems (see Skapska, 2003b: 69 ff.).
7 In the reality of post-communist societies, the human rights-oriented approach
seems closest to the definition of the law-governed state as victim-oriented. The effects
of such a conceptualization are morally to justify and honour individuals and groups who
resisted and fought against Stalinism. It presents, too, a foundation for the rehabilitation
of those who suffered under that regime and for the restitution of their rights (including
property).

179The Democratization and Modernization of Post-communist Judiciaries
— conceived by Westerners, built by Westerners, staffed with Westerners, and, by
all signs, efficiently and smoothly run by Westerners — is likely to remain for some
time a largely Western enterprise.”’ ce
In contrast to East Germany, there was no West Czechoslovakia; West Poland
or West Hungary that might have easily repudiated and replaced the legal ideology
and re-staffed judicial posts virtually overnight. But unlike East Germany, the rule
of law is building from within in Central and Eastern Europe. This process is still
underway, not yet completed, and post-socialist legislatures and lawyers are still
looking for a more precise model which they would like to develop and which
would best fit their societies. —
A first challenge to the ordinary judiciary came with the new demands that
the post-communist era put on all judges, in fact, on all lawyers. Many ordinary
judges as well as many academic lawyers tried to avoid this challenge by stressing
the difference between constitutional courts and ordinary courts, the former being
activist tribunals assigned the task of enforcing the constitution, the latter being only
mechanical agents who are supposed to read laws in a formalistic way. In effect,
they claimed that these new demands were placed solely on the constitutional
courts. The second, and even more important, challenge is coming now, with the
recent EU enlargement, when the ordinary judges have to begin the review of their
national government’s policies against the backdrop of the principles of EU law.
Suddenly, all judges started to encounter new problems with a vast political impact
and, in keeping with the doctrine expounded, they may not attempt to assign this
task solely to the constitutional courts.
This chapter, in a rather sketchy way, will show the trends in new laws on
the judiciary in the 1990s and 2000s and introduce the post-communist judges.
First, it will show the rise of pending cases after the fall of communism, a rise
which is limited by the abilities of post-communist judiciaries to handle caseloads
efficiently. Second, what happened to the ‘old’ judges will be discussed, including
the chronic lack of judges in the first post-communist decade and a gradual filling
of the judicial posts by the early 2000s. The third section analyses the problem of
judicial independence in Central Europe on paper and in reality. It also discusses
the personality of judges in Central Europe. The paper concludes with a brief
introduction to a post-communist judicial philosophy.
The Rise of Litigation
Since 1989, the rise in the rate of litigation, already visible towards the end of the
communist era, has accelerated. The number of cases at Hungarian district courts
increased by almost 50 per cent between 1991 and 1998; those before the regional

ordinary courts increased between 1990 and 2001 by 246 per cent.® Slovak district
judges faced a doubling in the annual number of new civil actions filed.'° In the
Czech Republic, between 1989 and 2000 the number of new civil actions filed in
civil district courts increased by approximately 30 per cent, the total number of
civil cases (both original and appellate) dealt with by regional courts doubled, and
the number of civil appeals to the same courts more than doubled. At the same time,
the number of serious crimes adjudicated by the Czech regional courts as courts
of first instance increased fivefold. In contrast, Czech district courts dealt with
approximately the same amount of criminal prosecutions as they did in the late
1980s." This difference might be accounted for by decriminalization of the socialist
era’s petty crimes, especially parasitism (which were decided by district courts),
and at the same time the emergence of complex cases of economic criminality,
which the regional courts must deal with as first instance courts. The increase of
litigation was accompanied by inevitable delays in deciding cases. These delays
are now a common problem throughout the post-communist region.”
However, there is a significant potential for the number of proceedings to
rise in the future, if the quality of judges improves. It seems that the insufficient
quality of the post-communist judiciary has kept this number lower than it would
otherwise have been. If developments in the former East Germany (GDR) after
1990 are compared with those in other post-communist countries of Central
Europe, a striking difference is revealed. After the Federal Republic of Germany
incorporated five new federal (formerly East German) Laender in 1990, thus
making available its efficient judiciary to persons living in the former GDR, they
have resorted to the judicial system far more often than have their counterparts in
other post-communist countries. In 1988 a total of 62,210 first-instance civil cases

Thus, the court administration which (in contrast to state administration of courts)
the Constitutional Court has been considering, is not, in content and regime,
distinguished from state administration nor from administration as such; thus,
it is unjustifiable to assert that the principle of superiority and subordination,
which is otherwise characteristic ef administration, does not apply within
its framework. It is an untenable notion that where the Ministry performs the
administration of courts through its chief judge, the court’s chief judge is not in
a relation of subordination towards the Ministry [...].
However, with regard to the selection of judges of ordinary courts, neither the
system with strong judicial councils nor the system with a strong executive
branch role appears to work much differently. First, the judicial autonomy which
increasingly pervades post-communist systems seems to support the inclination
towards a professional career judiciary (see the section on judges below). For
instance, the judges who exercise decisive functions within the Hungarian judicial
system, the most autonomous judicial system in the region and one of the most
autonomous in Europe, openly prefer young candidates without experience in
other legal professions over candidates with practice off the bench’ The situation
in the Czech Republic, the country strongly influenced by the Minister of Justice
and with no judicial council whatsoever, surprisingly goes in the same direction,
as the real power in selecting judges is exercised by chief judges of regional courts
and the actual role of the ministry is usually purely formal.
Although open politicization of the professional career model combined with
extensive judicial autonomy is unlikely, the negative side of this model is an
increasing insulation of the judiciary, which is generally considered unaccountable
and unresponsive to the needs of practical life.** Moreover, it seems to support
the tendency of law courts ‘to close ranks and resist substantive change’, as an
important Hungarian legal scholar put it.” Facing a uniform perspective on the

The Democratization and Modernization of Post-communist Judiciaries 197
methodology.” Analyses of the judiciaries in the post-communist region focus
mostly on the new and rapidly developing phenomenon of constitutional courts.
There are very interesting treatises describing the emergence and first decade of
the new constitutional judiciaries. More critical analysis of the post-communist
constitutional judiciaries has appeared recently. On the other hand, the
phenomenon of post-communist ordinary courts has been largely neglected, as the
novelty of constitutional courts has attracted all of legal scholars’ attention.
While post-communist law has been substantially modified since 1989, all too
often the methods of reasoning about that law remained unaffected. Considering
the fact that, to a substantial extent, the same persons continued in both judicial
offices and academic positions, this finding should come as no surprise.
It seems there were two periods in the development of communist legal style
and legal culture: first the Stalinism of the 1950s; and then the declining socialism
of the 1970s and 1980s."
The Stalinist conception of law suffered from an inner contradiction, as it
included both anti-formalist/activist and formalist/statist versions. If one were to
characterize Stalinist legal philosophy fully, it is fair to say that it was J anus-faced.
On the one hand, the era of Stalinism emphasized the activism of individuals
who were willing to achieve extraordinary working results and fight a foreign
enemy, Stalinist judges had to join this trend and they also had to show that they
contributed to the rapid building of socialism. Facing the specific atmosphere of
the time, judicial reasoning became surprisingly activist in all cases, not only in
political cases of the suppression of the opposition. In that period judicial reasoning
radically departed from its continental roots. On the other hand, however, the very
basic principles of Stalinist legal philosophy were remarkably formalist, dogmatic
and state-centred. Formalism of jurisprudence on the one hand and activist legal
reasoning on the other hand came into tension, and, after the end of Stalinism,
were finally resolved in favour of formalism.
What follows is the era of post-Stalinist dictatorships which, following Vaclav
Havel, can be referred to as ‘the post-totalitarian era’,® the era of allegedly
Marxist cliché to which, deep down, virtually nobody was committed. In this era
Socialist fervour died out everywhere, including in courtrooms, and survived only

202 Central and Eastern Europe After Transition
Viewed alone and separately from one another, none of these features suffices
to create a modern, bureaucratic system of adjudication.
Over the last two decades, Central and Eastern European judicial institutions
have undergone multiple processes of change (Kriger and Czarnota, 1999; Priba,
2001; Kiihn, 2004) in which domestic forces and international donors intensively
marked the pace and direction of judicial reforms (Dakolias, 1999; Morlino and
Magen, 2008; Piana, 2009).
Under their influence judicial institutions have endured two types of
transformation. The first one was aimed at de-politicizing judicial organizations
by introducing reliable mechanisms for the fair and transparent appointment of
judicial staff (Ptibafi, Roberts and Young, 2003). As a matter of fact, judges and
prosecutors appointed under communist rule were either kicked off the bench
or re-socialized in a new legal culture. The second transformation took place a
bit later on, when the bulk of legal reforms had already been realized and the
political systems were somehow moving toward their consolidation. At this
second stage, which overlapped with the pre-accession period, post-communist
countries embarked on a process of modernization which, in principle, asked
courts to develop new forms of expertise, including managerial know-how. The
core business of this second wave of reforms was more about capacity-building
than institutional design (Coman, 2007; Dallara, 2009). If, at first, post-communist
judicial systems had been asked to become impartial and to ensure their isolation
from politics, they were now being targeted by a number of policies aimed at
developing managerial know-how in its new members. In a nutshell, courts were
now also expected to pursue goals of efficiency and effectiveness.
The intertwining of these two transformations has been underexplored by
scholars (with few exceptions, such as Frydman, 2007; Piana, 2009). Though
deep and extensive empirical research should be conducted in order to properly
address this issue, by devoting attention to the type of values and logics of action
promoted by European institutions in post-communist judicial systems, one may
open a vista and provide a few clues about the knots left hanging by scholars on the
effects — whether intentional or not — that the pre-accession strategy had on these
systems. In trying to cast better light on the criticalities they are associated with,
the following pages will deal inevitably with four issues: (1) which consequences
might arise in Central and Eastern European countries from the implementation of
two different rationalities, one legal and the other managerial; (2) whether there
was anything specific about countries that were exiting from non-democratic
experiences or whether one could say that the same problems confronted by these
countries arise in advanced democracies as well; (3) to what extent it is legitimate
rationality, were expected to result in impartial and impersonal adjudication. According to
, this view, bureaucratic organizations of judicial roles should be able to protect magistrates
’ from undue influences and thereby guarantee impartial adjudication. Thus, as long as
judges adjudicate on the basis of law and behave as bureaucratic actors, legitimacy of the
adjudication is guaranteed.

Bureaucracy, Modernity and Judicial Governance in CEE Countries
In a bureaucratic judicial system, legal and bureaucratic logics of action — which
prescribe that decisions should be based on legal norms and should also be
respectful of the legal doctrine set down by senior judges and prosecutors usually
sitting in the high court (Cassation or Supreme) — co-participate to put in motion a
distinctive pattern ofjudicial governance inwhich the independence ofa single judge
is substantially subordinated to the independence of the magistracy as a system.
The rationale for this goes in the same direction as the principle of autonomy of
public administration from political institutions. As Max Weber correctly pointed
out, judges who work in bureaucratic settings benefit from very peculiar types of
guarantee, such as independence and professional status. Once recruited by means
of a general, standardized procedure (which very much resembles the procedure
adopted to recruit civil servants and bureaucrats) they are inserted into a machine
in which they will spend all of their careers. Each judge is expected to behave in
a way that is respectful of several different rules and standards. His behaviour
should be lawful and it should respect: the organizational values that constitute
and shape the identity of the judicial system in which they work; the professional
deontology of the legal professions; a standard of effectiveness and efficiency in the
use of the organizational resources; the rights of the citizens, the ultimate holders
of democratic sovereignty. ‘This complex picture figures out a situation where
judges expect costs and negative rewards if their behaviour does not respect a set
of several different standards. Some of them are weaker and informally enforced,
while some of them are harder and legally binding’ (Piana, 2009). One may safely
say that the bureaucratic judge (a judge who is working within a bureaucratically
organized judicial system) is held accountable by means of a vertical chain of
mechanisms of rule enforcement, whose effectiveness depends on the internal
cohesiveness of the judicial hierarchy.
What ensures the legitimacy ofa decision on a case is the balanced combination
ofaprocedurally correct process of: decision-making in relation to the case (evidence
taking, hearing of witnesses and so on) and the cohesiveness of the judicial
decisions taken in previous years/decades and among different courts belonging
to the same system. The consistency of the judicial hierarchy and the respect for
legal procedures are all aimed at ensuring the impartiality and imperturbability
of the bench vis-a-vis possible influences coming from the external environment,
whether politics, or society, or the market, or other foreign legal systems.
As we all know, this portrait no longer corresponds to the real state of affairs in
which adjudication takes place. Judges are now placed amidst a complex, multi-
layered and multi-centred global system, which generates norms that should be

accommodated mostly on a case-by-case basis rather than on the basis of deductive
and intra-systemic reasoning. Ordinary judges are allowed to be attentive to the
normative creation of foreign courts and, accordingly, to bypass or overrule the
doctrine endorsed by senior judges who are responsible for their own career
promotion. In issuing a sentence judges are no longer simply interested in domestic
reputation, but can be particularly sensitive to the reaction of foreign colleagues
he or she may have met during international meetings or seminars. It is not only
the legal procedure which starts to be in touch with ‘heteronomic’ inputs (that
is, inputs coming from different ‘nomos’, different normative orders), but also
the judicial hierarchy, who are put under pressure by the increasingly important
interaction of colleagues beyond the formalized borders of the bureaucracy in
which the hierarchy is embodied.
Non-democratic judicial systems fit into this picture with some nuances
and under specific conditions. It should be remembered, for example, that in
authoritarian regimes judges are usually not subjected to any particular form of
politicization, whereas the scope of their action is mostly and considerably reduced
by limiting the number and the types of cases on which ordinary courts adjudicate.
In this respect, the development of a hierarchical judicial organization is less
important for authoritarian rulers, because they do not aim to influence society
through adjudication. Sensitive cases and politically delicate issues are treated
outside the ordinary courts in special judicial bodies (military courts are a fairly
common example). Unlike authoritarian regimes, totalitarian regimes desperately
need the support of the bench in applying the law in line with the dominant (and
unique) ideology. Courts adjudicating under totalitarian rule are asked to become
part of the system rather than being left to one side (Arendt, 1951). Accordingly,
judicial behaviours are inclined to become over-proceduralized in order to mask,
through the sacred value of procedure (impersonal by definition), the arbitrariness
(from the point of view of citizens) of their decisions. Moreover, judicial hierarchy
is vital in the effective transformation of courts within the regime. The more
cohesive the hierarchy, the more value is injected into the system from the top
of the hierarchy, namely at the level of high-ranking judges, whose decisions are
more likely to be enforced along all levels of the judicial system, from supreme
courts to ordinary courts. Strong socialization to ideology is distinctive of this type
of system (Bihari, 1979 Lane, 1996). Whereas high-ranked judges are appointed
by political bodies, ordinary and low-ranked judges are often influenced by senior
colleagues and opportunities for career promotion (decided by senior judges).
Central and Eastern European countries are, in theory, representative of this
second model. With the passing of time, socialist states rapidly experienced
the collapse of authority and cohesiveness. Organizational units, in principle
belonging to the state, were in reality under the influence of external interests
and unable to stick to a common, organization-based set of values, due to the lack
of a fully-fledged impersonal approach. Therefore, in post-communist societies,
bureaucracies are in a very uneasy position. On the one hand, they are a vital
instrument for the processes of institutional change and institutional rebuilding

Polish Prosecutors, Political Corruption, and Legal Culture 247
Surrounded by Pressures, Opposing Expectations and Conflicting Norms
What emerges is a peculiar form of ‘telephone justice’ — an unofficial, informal
way of forcing justice out of court before it reaches the crucial phase of the
procedure in the courthouse. The preparatory, pre-trial part of the proceedings, as
one could expect, is ideal for exercising such justice through the use of personal
connections.
One may say that a specific ‘lex telefonicum’ is in force; that one makes a
decision based on an official command, or rather on consultation with a superior
prosecutor. Obviously, such cases of ‘telephone justice’ should not be treated
as endemic; they were even treated as exceptions by most of the interviewees.
However, such backstage justice may prevail and does prevail where political
interests (as in the case of Dr G., discussed below) or the interests of the highest-
ranking political patrons are at stake.
On one hand, prosecutors are under the constant control, sometimes even the
scrutiny, of their superiors and political patrons. On the other hand, they feel that
they are left alone when problems arise — for example, criticism, hostility from
politicians or the media, public outrage, and also the disapproval or discontent of
superiors (including the highest in the Appellate or State Prosecution, and, above
all, the Prosecutor-General) — they feel no support and no backing.
Mature democracies may resist such [political] pressures. It is much more
difficult, however. One might expect the outrage of a prosecutor who had been put
in such a situation to be much stronger, much more unequivocal, and one might
anticipate stronger resistance in such cases. Yet prosecutors in Poland are certain
that they will lose any confrontation they have with this political power. They
believe that, should they stamp their feet and say ‘no’, there would be nobody
standing behind them and nobody supporting them, all the support would be for
the politicians. Any daring decision they take must be taken alone.
Prosecutors Facing Media Scrutiny
A further topic for discussion amongst the interviewees was the role the media
play in the everyday work of prosecution. On one hand, participants stressed a
high level of journalistic scrutiny; though, unsurprisingly, it was perceived as a
problem. Yet, on the other hand, the interviewees felt that the quality of journalistic
professionalism and knowledge of the justice system was poor.
As stated, prosecutors complained about being under constant watch by the
media, which often brought them into the line of fire of public criticism.
I see the media’s role as negative. Media force special interest in a case on our
superiors. It’s all planned so they can write about what’s going on in the case,
while it should be enough that only me and my immediate superior is interested,
not anyone higher. Yet there is interest — of Regional Prosecution, Appellate and
State Prosecution, even from the Ministry of Justice in such media cases.

played a pivotal role. Yet, beyond the direct and collateral effects of these two
waves, EU institutions also had the opportunity to ‘accelerate’ a third epochal
mainstream that has been politically promoted by European unionism since the
Rome Treaty (1957), namely the ongoing ‘exhaustion’ of what was once called
‘nation-state building’. In other words, contrary to the amount of studies stressing
the rise of an all-encompassing ‘global law’, the historical sequence of these
three waves reveals a significant alteration of the already highly complex ‘unitas
multiplex’ of European legal experience: an alteration that also included one of its
most rewarded socio-legal patterns, that is, the cultural/technical, ‘professional |
mandate’ (Sarfatti Larson, 1989) of European legal professions as nation-state
builders, as Rudolf von Gneist once put it.
Indeed, legal professions’ traditional nation-state-oriented ‘Status Activae
Civitatis’ — that is, their unique legal position as ‘active citizens’ within the legal
system (Rebuffa, 1990) — can no longer be proclaimed a settled, unequivocal trait |
of European legal expertise at present (Olgiati, 1996a; 2007a). Besides, to the |
extent that the epistemic conditions of their traditional cultural identity, technical |
speciality and socio-political loyalty and commitment have been significantly de-
reconverted (Olgiati, 2001; 2003, 2009a), it is likely that their status-role will be
further reframed.
This being so, the aim of this study is to draw special attention to the theoretical
and practical relevance of such a context. To this end, some major contours of the
intertwined impact of the above-mentioned general waves on the European Union’s
province of law will be discussed. In particular, some exemplary experiences of
Eastern European legal professions will be outlined in order to make explicit the
link that exists between a given ‘Ratio Juris’ and the corresponding socio-legal
“power-knowledge’ knot.
The scientific relevance of the case of Eastern European socio-legal systems
and legal professions does not deserve to be stressed here. Instead, two additional
interrogatives are relevant. Given the contextual overlapping and entanglement of
the three above-mentioned waves, what sort of political, cultural and institutional
‘organizational brainstorming’ — otherwise called ‘transition’ — have they
experienced so far? And in what way, and to what extent, are they technically and
culturally ‘integrated’ into the current EU governance system?
As one can see, these questions raise a theoretical and practical problem whose
symbolic and operational implications have not been made explicit so far by
current legal and sociological literature. What kind of new common professional
‘Status Activae Civitatis’' will Eastern and Western European legal professions
be entitled to claim, in order to be legitimately recognized as veritable ‘boundary
agents’ between EU institutions and European society at large?
1 The ‘Status Activae Civitatis’ of \egal professions should not to be confused with the
notion of ‘active citizenship’ recently promoted among ordinary (lay) EU citizens to enable
them merely to participate in pre-constituted ‘deliberative’ proceedings and ‘subsidiary’
activities.

Owing to the complexity of the variables involved in dealing with the matter,
the concept of ‘positive entropy’, borrowed from scientific studies throwing light
on the relational co-evolution between energy, substance, space and time, will
be implicitly adopted, by analogy, as a leading frame of reference. Indeed, the
notion of ‘positive entropy’ outlines the fact that what we mean when we talk
about ‘order’ is an outcome of processes of internal reorganization accentuated
by external disorganizing inputs: processes that occur widely in contemporary
society and that, in many respects, seem to concern present-day EU law and
society interactions too.
Reframing the Study of European Professionalism
Leafing through scientific literature, one of the most remarkable problems for the
study of European professions at present is the assessment ofa theoretical approach
that may be considered not only analytically plausible (that is, intersubjectively
constructed through a rational argument), but also, and above all, socially adequate
(that is, grounded on primary claims and fundamental needs) (Luhmann, 1980).
Following what has been previously said, it is apparent that the issue at stake
lies precisely in what can be called the EU-driven ‘positive entropy’, that is, the
reorganization-through-disorganization of the European professional realm. This
was set in motion by the way in which EU governance dealt with each one of
the three epochal waves mentioned above, the socio-legal consequences being
such that it may be further involved, both in the short and long terms, at regional,
national and continental levels.
The multi-layered patterns of this ‘de-reconversion’ have already been discussed
elsewhere with reference to either legal professions (notaries, lawyers, judges)
(Olgiati, 1995a; 2000; 2007a) or the overall system of European learned professions
(Olgiati, 2001; 2008a). Two major difficulties in this respect came out: (1) how to
provide a detailed account of each professional variable while relating the topic to
the broader social context and vice versa; and (2) how to provide a reliable ‘order of
discourse’ to such a complex and thorough evolutionary mix of variables.
Given space-time constraints as well as the potentials of EU process and
policy, a critical distancing from currently dominating approaches to professions
and professionalism is required. In fact, an unprejudiced overview of the scientific
literature on contemporary European professions is sufficient to reveal what
otherwise should have been self-evident if these approaches had not acted — as
Braudel would put it — as veritable prisons du longue durée, that is, as mentally
stereotyped iron cages of such an extraordinary, historically new, unique character
of EU constitutional unionism. This is particularly true of the legal professions, as
they experienced, in their turn, a unique unprecedented change, pursued politically
‘from above’ and propelled technically, at the same time, as both a conscious socio-
technical Strukturbildung and a veritable ‘self-fulfilling prophecy’.
